title: Short Stuff: Laugh Tracks
summary: Short Stuff episode (sandwich edition tied to a two-part Sitcoms episode) on laugh tracks. Covers the origin of canned laughter with CBS sound engineer Charlie Douglas, who recorded laughter (including from Red Skelton and mime Marcel Marceau) and built the laugh box, a machine with reels of laughs, first used on The Hank McCune Show in 1950. Discusses how the laugh track was received as phony and corny, its heyday in the seventies, the announcement before a live studio audience, a 1960s focus group that favored a Hogan's Heroes pilot with a laugh track, Larry Gilbert's wish for MASH to have no laughs, laughter in Latin American TV, research suggesting laughter makes things seem funnier, and how shows like Seinfeld and later The Office moved away from laugh tracks. Ends with fan experiments watching sitcoms without laugh tracks and adding laugh tracks to non-comedy clips.

segments.title: Opening and laugh track origins
segments.summary: Hosts introduce laugh tracks (canned laughter) and their roughly 70-year history, explaining that CBS sound engineer Charlie Douglas began recording laughter to fix inconsistent live audiences.

segments.title: The laugh box and first laugh track
segments.summary: Douglas recorded laughter from performers such as Red Skelton and Marcel Marceau, and his first laugh track debuted in 1950 on The Hank McCune Show. He built the laugh box, a filing-cabinet-sized machine with about 32 reels and up to 320 laughs that could be played like an instrument, which he called the audience response duplicator.

segments.title: Reception and the seventies heyday
segments.summary: Laugh tracks were derided as phony and corny, and Douglas became reclusive. The laugh track peaked in the seventies, when shows used a disclaimer before live studio audience. Scooby Doo and the Flintstones and Jetsons also used laugh tracks.

segments.title: Hogan's Heroes focus group, MASH, and international laughers
segments.summary: A mid-1960s CBS focus group reportedly preferred a Hogan's Heroes pilot with a laugh track, cementing the practice. MASH creator Larry Gilbert wanted no laughs but kept a laugh track outside surgery scenes. Latin American shows reportedly hired professional laughers.

segments.title: Laughter research and the decline of laugh tracks
segments.summary: Research suggests people find things funnier with canned laughter, reportedly 15 to 20 percent. Seinfeld used a laugh track into the nineties, while the UK version of The Office helped turn the tide against them because its cringe comedy would not work with one.

segments.title: Sitcoms without laugh tracks and fan edits
segments.summary: Hosts discuss watching classic sitcoms like Friends without laugh tracks, which feels disjointed and less funny to them, and mention a Ross clip with the laugh track removed. They also talk about fan-made laugh track additions to non-comedy clips such as Space Ghost.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and note the company's podcast information.
